It's June 2035. Ludwig is turning 87. Lena has organised a party in the courtyard. Elif has invented a game: each guest writes an adjective about Ludwig on a slip of paper. Ludwig reads the slips.
Right, Mr Brandt. Here are thirty-seven slips of paper. On each one there's an adjective about you. You have to guess who wrote what.
Thirty-seven? I hope they're all friendly. The first: “patient”. That was Leo. Because I listen to him every evening when he talks about his driving lessons.
“humorous”. That was Hotte. No, wait, Hotte would have written “daft”. That was Andrei.
That's right. And this one's from me: “stubborn”. Because at eighty-seven you still won't admit you need reading glasses.
I don't need glasses. I just need longer arms. Next: “reliable”. That was Kurt Wolff. Definitely. He's never forgotten that I left him waiting in the snow.
And this one? It's very long.
“Tireless-patient-generous-modest”. That's four adjectives, Elif, it's against the rules. That was Susanne. A woman who can't make up her mind.
And the last one? You're not reading it aloud.
The last one is… “irreplaceable”. No name. In handwriting I don't recognise.
It was Grete. She dictated it to me yesterday because her hand shakes too much. She said I shouldn't tell. But today's your birthday.
Irreplaceable. That's a big word. From a woman who is irreplaceable herself.
to tell (a secret), to give away
“-los” and “-voll” are often opposite pairs: hoffnungslos / hoffnungsvoll, respektlos / respektvoll, wertlos / wertvoll.
Many -lich adjectives from verbs take “un-”: unvergesslich, unersetzlich, unermüdlich, unaufhaltsam.
Not every adjective takes “un-”. You don't say “ungroß” or “unalt”, but “klein” and “jung”. “un-” mainly appears with derived adjectives.
4. How to describe someone with nuance
Er ist nicht nur humorvoll, sondern auch sehr bescheiden.

“alles andere als” = anything but. It's an elegant way of expressing the opposite of a quality.
She's very thrifty: she spends little money.
He wasn't patient, he was impatient.
Adjective from “essen” meaning “that can be eaten”:
He's not only humorous but also modest.
He's the most helpful person I know.

Ludwig's eighty-seventh birthday fell on a Saturday in June, a warm, cloudless day on which the old chestnut tree in the courtyard of Kastanienallee thirty-one was in full bloom, with hundreds of white candles among its big green leaves. Lena had been planning the party in secret for weeks, with a list as long as the lists Elif made for her signature campaigns. The problem was that Ludwig hated surprises. He said so every year. “Anyone who surprises me,” he used to say, “is risking my heart attack. And then the party's over anyway.”

So Lena had told him there would be a little coffee in the courtyard on Saturday, just the family, just one cake. Ludwig had nodded suspiciously. He knew his granddaughter. But he wasn't prepared for what he saw when, at three on Saturday afternoon, in his good grey shirt, leaning on his stick, he came out through the back door into the courtyard. Under the flowering chestnut tree stood three long tables, and at the tables sat thirty-seven people, and when they saw him they all stood up at once and sang, out of tune and loudly, in German, in Romanian, in Turkish and in Berlin dialect: “Happy birthday!”

Ludwig stood speechless in the doorway. He looked at them all, one after another. Thomas and Anja from Treptow, with Marie, who had come specially from Munich, and Paul, who had even come from Vienna. Leo in his BVG uniform, straight from his shift. Sabine from Potsdam, with a home-made cake. Mara and Jakob, with little Ingrid Hilde in a baby wrap, four months old, the only one not singing but sleeping. Andrei and Lena. The Yilmaz family. Susanne from Hanover and Mirko from Dresden, together, with his viola. Michael Kühn, the landlord. Kurt Wolff from the Tram Museum. Mrs Krause from the district office, in a private capacity. Katrin Krüger, without her notebook. And at the end of the third table, on the best chair, with his old tram driver's cap on his head: Hotte.

Only one was missing. Grete hadn't come. She had been tired for a week, very tired, Mrs Petersen from the care home had said on the phone, and the doctor had advised her to stay in bed. She was ninety-nine. In May she had celebrated her birthday in a small circle, without the piano, because her hands shook too much. She had said she would be there at Ludwig's party, “at least with one word”. Ludwig didn't know then what she meant. He only found out in the evening, when he read the last of the thirty-seven slips.

There was cake, of course. Andrei had baked a cake that looked like an old Tatra tram, red and beige, with the number 46 on one side and eighty-seven little candles on the roof. Sabine had brought a cheesecake made to Ingrid's recipe, which she had found in an old cookbook. Ayşe Yilmaz brought baklava. Mrs Lorenz had sent an onion tart by post from Thuringia, which had suffered a bit on the way but was eaten anyway. And Hotte had brought a bottle without a label, containing a clear liquid that he claimed was “medicine from the depot, vintage 1972”. Nobody dared to try it except Dan, who happened to be visiting from Sibiu and who, after the first glass, said in Romanian that it was almost as good as his țuică (plum brandy).

After the cake, Hotte stood up, tapped his glass with a teaspoon and gave a speech nobody had asked for. It was in Berlin dialect, of course, and lasted twelve minutes, and Lena whispered a translation to Dan, who still understood only half. “I've known Ludwig since nineteen sixty-eight,” Hotte began. “Back then he was twenty and I was twenty-three, and he was the only one at the depot who came on time. That was suspicious. I thought he was Stasi. But no. He was just orderly.” The whole courtyard laughed. Then Hotte told how, in the winter of nineteen seventy-nine, at minus twenty degrees, Ludwig had stopped the tram because an old woman with two heavy shopping bags was running too slowly towards the stop, and how he had got out and carried her bags, and how the inspector had given him a warning for it. “And do you know what he said to the inspector?” Hotte shouted. “He said: the timetable is there for the people. Not the people for the timetable.”

Then came Elif's game. She had given every guest a white slip of paper and a pen, and each of them had written a single adjective about Ludwig on it, without a name, then folded the slip and put it in an old tin box Lena had brought from Ludwig's kitchen. Ludwig had to read every slip and guess who it was from. It took two hours. It was, as Katrin Krüger said later, the most beautiful portrait of a person she had ever heard, and she had written a lot of them in thirty years.

“Patient”, from Leo. “Humorous”, from Andrei. “Stubborn”, from Lena, and everyone laughed. “Reliable”, from Kurt Wolff. “Generous”, from Michael. “Curious”, from Katrin Krüger. “Tireless-patient-generous-modest”, from Susanne, against the rules. “Brave”, from Mara, who explained that at eighty-six you have to be brave to go to the hospital at night because a baby is coming. “Taciturn”, from Hotte, and then the whole courtyard laughed, because everyone knew that Ludwig was many things, but anything but taciturn, and that was exactly why Hotte had written it.

Some slips Ludwig couldn't guess. “Warm” was from Mrs Yilmaz, who said very quietly that Ludwig had been the first German to greet her in the street twenty-one years ago, with a smile, when she didn't know a single word of German yet. “Helpful” was from Mirko, who remembered how Ludwig had straightened his tie at the Konzerthaus before the concert. “Unforgettable” was from Thomas. Ludwig read it twice. Then he looked at his son, who was sitting at the other end of the table pretending to stir his coffee with great interest. Ludwig said nothing. He folded the slip and put it in his shirt pocket, over his heart.

Between the slips, Mirko played the viola, softly, under the chestnut tree. He didn't play a concert piece but old Berlin songs that Ludwig had heard from his mother as a child, and during one of them, a song about the Spree and the moon, Ludwig sang along, in his deep, slightly cracked voice, and Mrs Schulze, who at ninety-two was sitting at the first table, sang the second part. Little Ingrid Hilde woke up, looked around with big, serious eyes and apparently decided that everything was all right, because she went straight back to sleep. Jakob said later that it had been his daughter's first concert and that she had sat through it with great patience. “Patient,” said Ludwig. “She gets that from me. We're not related, but still.”

The last slip was written in handwriting Ludwig didn't recognise, round and neat, a child's handwriting. But the word on it wasn't a child's word. “Irreplaceable”, it said. And underneath, very small, in the same child's handwriting, a note that broke all the rules of the game: “Dictated by G. H., who can't come because her legs have gone on strike. But her head is here.” Ludwig held the slip in his hand for a long time. Elif explained quietly how she had been at Grete's bedside the evening before, and how Grete had dictated the word to her, letter by letter, with her eyes closed. “She said it's the only adjective she's used just twice in ninety-nine years,” said Elif. “Once for Friedrich. And once for you.”

The courtyard went quiet. Not even Hotte said anything. Ludwig stood up, slowly, leaning on his stick, and looked across the three tables, across the thirty-seven faces, across the chestnut tree with its white candles of blossom. Then he said, and his voice wasn't quite steady: “Today I've been given thirty-seven adjectives. Thank you for every one. But I have to tell you something. I'm not irreplaceable. Nobody is. The only irreplaceable thing is this.” He pointed with his stick across the courtyard, across the tables, across the people. “What you've done in this house. On this street. That's irreplaceable. And that will stay, even when I'm no longer here.”

Nobody knew what to say to that. Then Leo stood up, in his BVG uniform, and pulled the cord of the old brass bell, which Lena had brought specially from the café into the courtyard for the day. It rang twice. Not once, as when a baby arrives, but twice, the way the old tram drivers at the depot did when one of them had a particularly hard shift behind him. Hotte took off his tram driver's cap and held it to his heart. And then the whole courtyard applauded, for a long time, and Ludwig sat back down and pretended he had got something in his eye, a chestnut blossom, maybe, that had fallen from the tree.

Late in the evening, when most of the guests had gone and only the fairy lights in the chestnut tree were still glowing, Ludwig went to the care home with Mara and Elif. It was almost ten, but Mrs Petersen let them in. Grete lay in bed, her eyes closed, very small under the white blanket. When Ludwig sat down beside her, she opened her eyes and looked at him, with her clear gaze that was still a little ironic. “Well,” she whispered. “Did they praise you nicely?” Ludwig took her hand. “Thirty-seven times,” he said. “But yours was the most beautiful.” Grete smiled. “I know,” she whispered. “I thought about it for a long time.” Then she closed her eyes again, and Ludwig stayed sitting there, with her hand in his, until she fell asleep.
